style_when: the story is a single number, rule, gate or shift and restraint is the point — with no scene to photograph, the frame must still be a real assembly: a modular bay, an unlatched inspection gate, a rack of blades, an interlocking connector
prompt: A modular yard robot staged on a weathered concrete garage floor: a low tracked core unit parked off-centre on the right third, its mower module half-docked on top, a snow-blower module and a blower module standing in a receding row to the left like rungs of a ladder. Matte textured polymer shells in deep pine green and graphite, galvanised steel tracks, hard clean edges, moulding seams. A single low raking key light from the open garage door on the left throws one long cast shadow across the concrete; muted graphite and ochre palette, generous negative space above, matte muted finish, no text.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, numbers, watermarks, logos
rationale: The article turns on a single number and a modular machine, which is exactly the component_assembly trigger: restraint stating the idea. The three recognisable yard-robot parts in one deliberate row make the bundle — and every module that raises the payment — the hero, in the garage where the machine actually lives.
subject: A modular yard robot's tracked core unit with its mower, snow-blower and blower modules staged in a receding row on a garage floor
core_thesis: Yarbo's own financing puts its full four-module yard robot bundle at $774.92 a month, more than the $300–$520 a landscaping crew bills for a one-acre lawn, so year one of owning costs more than year one of hiring.
core_conflict: The robot's flat monthly installment versus the crew's seasonal invoice — owning priced above hiring in year one, with payback only possible if the machine survives to year two and replaces both mowing and plowing.
composition: Asymmetric off-centre framing: core unit parked on the right third, modules receding left in a ladder row, one long cast shadow, generous negative space above
